title: Dependency Parsing
oneLiner: Describe a sentence as arrows between words, from each word to the words that depend on it, and learn to draw those arrows fast or optimally.

what.html:
Dependency parsing links each word to the word it depends on: the subject and object hang off the verb, "the" hangs off its noun. The result is a tree of labelled arrows. Parsers build it either step by step with a stack and a queue (fast, greedy) or by scoring every possible arrow and picking the best whole tree (slower, global).

Everyday versionThe main verb is the sun; nouns are planets pulled by it; little words like "the" are moons around the nouns. Every word is pulled by exactly one other word.

why.html:
• Arrows say directly who did what to whom, which is ideal for extracting facts.
  • They work even when word order is free (Hindi, Russian).
  • Ambiguities become a single arrow choice.

how.title: Order changes, relations don't
how.html: In Hindi, "Ram gave Sita a book" can be said in several orders because little markers carry the roles. The arrows from "gave" to each noun stay the same.

how.title: Arrows with labels
how.html: Each arrow goes from head to dependent with a label like subject or object. "I saw a girl with a telescope" hinges on one arrow: from "saw" or from "girl" to "with".

how.title: Rules for a proper tree
how.html: Every word has exactly one head, there are no loops, everything connects to the root, and usually no arrows cross.

how.title: One label set for all languages
how.html: Universal Dependencies uses the same relation names (subject, object, adjective modifier, determiner…) across 100+ languages.

how.title: Four ways to parse
how.html: Fill a table like CKY, delete impossible arrows, make greedy step-by-step moves, or search for the best-scoring tree.

how.title: The assembly line
how.html: Words wait on a conveyor (buffer) next to a workbench (stack). Four moves (shift, left-arc, right-arc, reduce) attach them one by one: "He sent her a letter ." takes ten moves.

how.title: Learning which move to make
how.html: A classifier looks at the stack top and buffer front and picks a move. When it is wrong in training, add the correct move's features to its weights and subtract the wrong move's. Fast, but an early mistake can't be undone.

how.title: The best whole tree
how.html: Score every possible arrow, let each word pick its best head, and fix any loops by merging them and re-scoring. For "John saw Mary" the best tree scores 70: root → saw → John and Mary.

demo.html: Introduce a wrong label or a wrong head into the parse of "He sent her a letter ." and watch the two standard scores: the share of words with the right head (UAS) and with the right head and label (LAS).

example.html:
Breaking a loop. In "John saw Mary", John picks "saw" (30) and "saw" picks John (20): a loop. Merge them; entering the merged node through "saw" from the root is worth 10 − 20 + 50 = 40, better than through John (29). So the root points to "saw", and the John → saw arrow is dropped.

Supplementary Parsers are scored by the share of words with the correct head (UAS) and with the correct head and label (LAS).

misunderstandings: Arrows point from dependent to head.
Crossing arcs occur, especially with free word order.
They're greedy: one action at a time.
Greedy picking of best heads always gives a tree.
It can create cycles; CLE fixes them.
takeaways: Dependencies: head → dependent with a label; suits free word order.
Valid trees: connected, acyclic, single head; usually projective.
UD: shared relations (nsubj, obj, amod, det…).
Arc-eager: SH, LA, RA, RE; linear time; perceptron-trained oracle.
Graph-based: maximum spanning tree with Chu-Liu-Edmonds (John saw Mary = 70).
thirty: Dependency grammar links words by head → dependent arcs with labels, like a solar system around the main verb; it handles free word order (Hindi case markers) and reduces PP attachment to one arc (saw → with vs girl → with). Trees are connected, acyclic and single-headed, usually projective. Universal Dependencies standardises relations (nsubj, obj, iobj, amod, det, obl:tmod). Parsers: dynamic programming (Eisner O(n³)), constraint satisfaction, transition-based, graph-based. Arc-eager uses configuration (stack, buffer, arcs) and SH/LA/RA/RE; 'He sent her a letter .' takes 10 actions; a classifier (perceptron: w += f(c, t_o) − f(c, t*)) chooses actions greedily in O(n), with error cascades. Graph-based parsing finds the MST: Chu-Liu-Edmonds picks best incoming arcs, contracts cycles (root→C = 10 − 20 + 50 = 40), recurses and unpacks: root→saw, saw→John, saw→Mary = 70; learning updates globally.
